narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, well below the average of accepted students who typically rank around the sixth and fifth-to-sixth deciles. These low academic standings in law school were the main reasons the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA also mattered, but worked in the opposite direction. Both scores were slightly below the average of accepted students (35 versus 37.2 on the LSAT, and 2.9 versus 3.23 GPA), yet they still provided a modest pull toward passing. Unfortunately, these positive signals were not strong enough to overcome the much larger negative impact of your class rankings.

You should focus on improving your academic performance if you retake courses or enroll elsewhere, and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Strengthening these areas will give you the best chance of a favorable prediction next time. (218 words)
